title: Your right is to the work: Gita 2.47
hookLine: Arjuna drops his bow, and Krishna answers with a line about the work and its fruit
carry: karma yoga: do the work, offer the fruit
tomorrow: would you give up heaven for a dog?

cards: On the field of Kurukshetra, two armies wait. Arjuna, the finest archer there, asks Krishna, his charioteer, to drive out between them. He looks across and sees his teachers, his cousins, his own grandfather.
His bow slips from his hand. He sinks down in the chariot and says: I will not fight.
Krishna's answer becomes the Bhagavad Gita, and in its second chapter comes a line millions know by heart: karmaṇy evādhikāras te, mā phaleṣu kadācana.

teach.h: YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE WORK.
teach.b: Its sense, in paraphrase: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your motive, and don't cling to doing nothing either. This is the heart of karma yoga, the path of action.
Arjuna isn't told to stop caring, or to stop acting. He's told to do what is his to do, fully, and to let go of his grip on how it turns out. A verse later, the Gita calls that evenness yoga.
And later still, Krishna takes it one step further: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, do it as an offering to me.

That's why many Hindus, finishing a task, a meal or a puja, quietly say Krishnarpanam astu: let this be offered to Krishna. The work is given, and the fruit goes with it. Now hear how the line is built.
Karmaṇy: the ṇ curls back. Evādhikāras is two words joined: eva, alone, and adhikāraḥ, right. The two a's merge into a long ā, and the visarga becomes an s because a t comes next.
The Taittiriya's old list of the parts of sound calls this kind of thing santana, the joining.
Mā phaleṣu: ph is a p that breathes, never an f.

teach.h: KRISHNARPANAM ASTU: LET IT BE OFFERED.

teach.b: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te, mā phaleṣu kadācana.
None of this is needed to love the line; the Gita can be held close in any language.

teach.h: DO THE WORK. OFFER THE FRUIT.
teach.b: But the line makes its own point: say it carefully, as an offering, and let how it sounds to anyone else go.

how: Many Hindus learn Gita 2.47 by heart, and on finishing a task, a meal or a puja quietly say Krishnarpanam astu, "let this be offered to Krishna"; students learn to recite the verses line by line with a teacher, attending to how the words join.

o: a long pause taken between two lines of verse
the ending a word takes when it stands alone
the joining: sounds that change where words meet

games.q: the work and its fruit — tap the pairs.
p: your right is to the work alone
let this be offered to Krishna

s: Krishna tells Arjuna to stop caring and stop acting
he's told to act fully without clinging to the fruit, and not to cling to doing nothing either.
in the Gita, whatever you do can be offered to God
Krishna says: whatever you do, eat or give, do it as an offering to me.
the ph in phaleṣu is said like f
it's a p with a puff of breath.

games.q: Arjuna has dropped his bow and won't fight. what does Krishna's well-known line in chapter two tell him?
o: your right is to the outcome, so make sure you win.
your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits.
walk away: doing nothing is safest.
games.why: do what's yours to do, fully, without gripping the result, and don't cling to doing nothing either. that's karma yoga.

practice: Say the line one piece per breath: karmaṇy; evādhikāras, holding the long ā; te; mā; phaleṣu, letting the ph breathe; kadācana. Then bring to mind one piece of work whose result you're still waiting on.
If you pray, offer it, in words like Krishnarpanam astu, and leave it there. If you don't, simply set it down: your part is done. Sit a few breaths with your hands open.

wordCard.voice: Santana. The joining: words that lean into each other, as eva and adhikāraḥ do in the Gita's line on the work and its fruit.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: karmaṇy evādhikāras te, Gita 2.47, written as one joined string.

carryVoice: Your line: karma yoga: do the work, offer the fruit. Tomorrow, the year's last block opens on a mountain road. See you then.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.26–47 and 2.9 (Arjuna sees his kin and will not fight)
